entries.text: Tape 13-A. Interview with David Gould and Gary Vonderohe by Bob Zybach while touring the Elliott State Forest on October 10, 2018. Part 1. Trout Creek to Jacobson Fishing Hole to Elkhorn Ranch (46:57)
#D-01. 0:10 Trout Creek Fry, Waterfalls & Landslides. Photos (2): 1012; 1013

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Gary, you said you saw some fish up here.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Yeah. I don't know if they're cutthroat or juvenile coho. Something. You know, something ... a juvenile salmonid.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh-huh.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: It's named Trout Creek, so it's probably trout.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So, and there's probably been trout for a while. We're looking at here the result of the landslide and the gravel that's now in there?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I was just trying to find out the gravels coming out of the hill, out of the landslides, and it's coming out into the streams, and then redistributed and clean sorted out by the water and it gets the sand and stuff out of it, makes gravel for the fish to spawn in. The sand and dirt looking stuff goes on towards the ocean and you get the gravel, you know, it comes out of the hills.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So it's Trout Creek, it's been called Trout Creek for a while, but the landslide is only 2 or 3 years ago. Do you think there's been a history of just constant landslides through this area?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Well of course there has, that's why [inaudible 00:01:11].

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: There's another- see it's right here, I don't think you can see it-

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: That right there?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Right there, that's another place where the water comes down in a landslide and it came right in over that. See all these trout there? Come straight out across the road and mud went down the ditch and cleaned that up. That all had gravel in it and that's how you're getting the gravel out in these streams. It's coming out the hills. There's no road up there where that come out of. That's just natural. Come right out of the hill.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Jerry's information showed that they had a whole lot of landslides over a ten-year period in the 60's, and then not so much for ten or twenty years, then a bunch in the 80's again. Does that seem right to you from your experience?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That's true, that's when they had the farms. You can't quite see it down here but there's a waterfall down in the main area down there. I'm not sure fish could get over that. I don't know I am going to walk down and slip.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: There's a waterfall below us, but there's trout above the waterfall.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So, how does that happen?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Well they get up through it. They swim through it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So, the waterfall isn't a barrier to the fish.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Gary does that fit in with what you've seen, what you've learned about this country? Natural landslides occur pretty regularly and keep this gravel in the streams.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Yeah definitely, some trees, where you might have a small cluster of trees that will sluff off. Then it will cause a small landslide and you can see it on some of the hillsides. You can see the gravel coming in.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So, the landslides are pretty critical at some level for creating habitats.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Yeah, it is something that naturally happened. It's what's natural vs. in some places you get mass landslides, mass wastes, that type of thing. Which, still provides gravel but there's a lot more negative effects of that to fish. Versus these natural ones which are just kind of trickling in gravel.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So on the mass landslides, is the reason it's negative for fish because it blocks access to the stream? Is that the main problem or sedimentation?

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Yeah, you've got a little of both. Usually the blockage is short, typically short term. But I've seen it somewhere when it really blocks a lot. Not necessarily in the Coos basin, but somewhere like the Tenmile basin. But then there's more of that sedimentation for a few years. You get that long- term sedimentation. A lot of silt that can suffocate eggs.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: In the wintertime, fish can have a hard time feeding because of it.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: You might drive around on the [inaudible 00:04:52].

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: These are pretty steep hills so meanders aren't that common are they?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Not really, but in the lower part. There's one down there by Stalls Bridge. [inaudible 00:05:19] There's one of them down there. Then there's a lot of sliding. There used to be a bridge down there. Then [inaudible 00:05:45]. You see that? Plenty meanders down below.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: It might be down just a little ways.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: There should be some fish down there.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: No, the adult one there. Basically the trout there. I think that that's the lowest we've done.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: [inaudible 00:06:39] We're out here walking over them. [inaudible]
#D-02. 7:12 West Fork Spawning Gravel to New Beaver Dam. Photos (8): 1018; 1019; 1020; 1022; 1023; 1024; 1025; 1026

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So now we're on the West Fork, are we heading toward the Elkhorn Ranch?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Yeah back there is where they come. [inaudible 00:07:44]

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Are you familiar with the history of this area through here, Gary?

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Just a little bit. I'm sure there is a lot more to learn.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: You see the gravel down below. You see gravel over there. That's been like this for 30 years. I've got photos of all over here. It shows more gravel here. It comes down from quite a ways.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Yeah. It all got started a couple of years ago.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Let me get a picture or two here, David. I could just leave this in here if you want to describe what we're looking at.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Alright well we can step right out. There's a lot of gravel on the bottom of this thing.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You got the recorder right here by your elbow.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: That gravel right there stems from way up the river. This last winter got it in here. It's kind of unique. They're probably six miles below the source of where it came from.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Let me get my recorder here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So David, you're saying this area here, that just got photographed, didn't have any spawning gravel in it.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: No, it came down probably five miles above here. That slide came down and now the Millicoma Meander timber sales caused a washout.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: The washout caused of the quarry about 25 hundred to 3,000 yards of material into the river. Then there's all the washout and it put rocks and material right into the river.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: When that happened did they blame it on the logging, the landslide or was that just coincidental?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: What the deal was that the rock when down into the water. Then the logs got loose and came pushing all the gravel into the river. They came and took out all the big rocks and the other stuff worked its way down. That's how you got a bunch of gravel in the river is by the logging.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Gary, are you familiar with the history of that landslide that he's talking about?

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: I am not sure if that is the same one I know of.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well, what we're looking at, this looks to me like pretty positive habitat.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Yeah there's a lot of good gravel here that's for spawning for salmonids or for lamprey.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The lamprey make it up here?

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Yeah, there's a lot of lamprey in the West Fork of the Millicoma.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Do people still call them eels here? You correct them do you?

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: They still do.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Eel Creek, Eel Lake.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Another thing we've found through here is Millicoma Dace, which is a dace species but it's kind of diverged from Longnose Dace. It's only found in the Coos basin.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: What's that?

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Like a minnow but it sits in the cobbles. So you find them in those cobbles with the faster moving water and they are very site specific. I know I have sampled through here and we've found them here.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: There's some over there along the bank.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Then there's Speckled Dace, which are kind of a relative, a different species.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Before this gravel got in here, there was still fish in here though.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: There's fish, yeah. But it was just like a bedrock shelf. I have fished through here in the winter for steelhead.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So the fishing are moving through here but before the gravel they couldn't spawn.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: They didn't spawn here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But now they could.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: There's potential if things are right. Just because there's gravel here doesn't mean it's right for a fish to spawn.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Uh huh.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: If the hydrology is perfect, there's enough flow. Usually it would be back here in the tail-out would be the place you'd think you'd see most of them spawning.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The gravel up here on the bank, it not only had to be covered here at the right time of year for two or three weeks for the fish to spawn and to hatch?

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Right but they have to be in the right water. [inaudible 00:13:46]

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Do you know anything about that, Gary, when the water is up higher, then the bank gravel, does that increase the potential for it?

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: As long as it stays wet.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: For three or four weeks?

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Yeah, then then fry can get out. If the stuff up there by the bank dries, fish aren't necessarily going to use that or the chances are the ones that do, their eggs aren't going to survive.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So with the water coming in, that stuff up there with the grass on that, that becomes potential spawning habitat?

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: Yeah, it can.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: Just up the creek there, it's good for something.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Let's get located on a map too, for these stops here. I'm keeping this running as long as you're still talking.

entries.speaker: Gary Vonderohe
entries.text: [inaudible 00:15:16] I've seen videos that people have made, on Youtube, where people are driving up this road going to the flats, driving through the big mud holes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They put videos of this area there? They've got mud runners back there at the camp, or that camp right in front of us. Can you find on the map one or two stops here. It will be recorded on the photograph. There's two maps here.

entries.speaker: David Gould
entries.text: I haven't looked at a map in a while.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah I wanted USGS 7.5 minute quadrangle maps for this the first time. Amber just made these maps as we went. So, we've got this. Thank you.
